meta.title: Words in context · the committee that would not move

source.usage_note: Words from the CAT high-frequency list (content/lexicon); every sentence, option and explanation composed for CAT OS. Personal study only.

meta.reviewer_notes: The word bank's opening bundle: ten high-frequency words, each inside a sentence that forces one sense, with the commonest other sense, a near-synonym at the wrong strength and the opposite the sentence invites as the three traps.

quality.adversarial_review: Item 3 (laconic): 'They went.' could be heard as contemptuous, so the contempt option is the live rival; it fails because the sentence gives no evidence of scorn, only of brevity — the two-word reply is the whole clue. Item 6 (languish): 'deteriorated in quality' is a real sense of the word; it fails because the sentence describes a proposal's status ('neither rejected nor advanced'), not its quality. Item 10 (sardonic): 'reluctant' captures some of the discomfort but not the mockery the situation implies; the sentence's 'after all' points at irony.

items.stem: For three days the committee remained inert, receiving memoranda and returning none, until the minister's own letter arrived.

options.B: inactive, making no move in response

explanation.clue: The clause after the word tells you what 'inert' looks like here: 'receiving memoranda and returning none' — things come in, nothing goes out.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The committee does nothing in response to what it receives; that is inactivity, and the minister's letter is what finally moves it. The sentence describes passivity, not resistance.

distractors.why_wrong: The chemical sense is real, but a committee is not a substance; the sentence uses the word's extended sense of not moving or acting.
Hostility would be an action; the committee takes none. The sentence describes an absence of response, not opposition.
Nothing in the sentence concerns secrecy; returning no memoranda is inaction, not concealment.

explanation.method: Look for the clause that shows the word in action. A description that follows a colon or a comma usually restates the word in plain terms; match that, not the word's most familiar dictionary sense.

items.stem: No one impugned the accountant's figures; what the board questioned was the motive behind releasing them so early.

options.A: cast doubt on the truth or honesty of

explanation.clue: The semicolon sets up a contrast: nobody did X to the figures, but the board did question the motive. X must be a kind of questioning — of the figures themselves.
explanation.correct_reasoning: To impugn is to challenge as false or dishonest. The sentence says the figures' truth was not challenged; only the timing's motive was. The parallel between 'impugned' and 'questioned' is the giveaway.

distractors.why_wrong: The structure 'no one … what the board questioned was …' contrasts two kinds of doubt, so the missing sense must be a form of doubt, not praise.
Examining figures is neutral; impugning them attacks their integrity. The sentence contrasts an attack on the figures with a question about motive.
The figures were released, so concealment cannot be what nobody did to them.

explanation.method: When a sentence is built on 'not X; rather Y', the unknown word is a sibling of Y — the same kind of thing, applied to a different object.

items.stem: Asked how the negotiations had gone, the ambassador was laconic: 'They went.'

options.A: deliberately vague, to avoid committing herself
options.C: speaking at length about trivial matters

explanation.clue: The reply is quoted: two words. The sentence shows you the word's meaning instead of telling you.
explanation.correct_reasoning: Laconic describes speech that uses the fewest possible words. 'They went' is the demonstration — brevity is the whole of what the sentence reports about the ambassador.

distractors.why_wrong: The reply may be uninformative, but the word describes its length, not its purpose; nothing in the sentence says the ambassador was avoiding commitment.
A two-word answer can sound dismissive, but the sentence gives no sign of scorn; laconic is about economy of words, and carries no contempt of its own.
This is the opposite of what the quoted reply shows.

explanation.method: When a sentence quotes the speech it is describing, the quotation is the definition. Describe the quotation in plain words before you look at the options.

items.stem: The auditor listed the venial lapses first — a receipt misfiled, a date left blank — and saved the matter of the missing funds for the end.

explanation.clue: The dashes give examples — a misfiled receipt, a blank date — and the sentence contrasts them with 'the missing funds', kept for the end. The examples are trivial; the contrast is with the grave.
explanation.correct_reasoning: Venial means pardonable, slight. The auditor's ordering — small lapses first, the serious matter last — and the examples themselves both point at minor faults.

distractors.why_wrong: A misfiled receipt and a blank date are carelessness, not concealment; nothing suggests these lapses were hidden.
This is the meaning of 'venal' (open to bribery), a look-alike word. The examples given have nothing to do with corruption.
The sentence contrasts these lapses with the missing funds, so they are the lesser faults, not the unforgivable ones.

explanation.method: Examples set off by dashes are the writer glossing the word for you. Rate the examples — trivial or grave — and choose the sense at that level.

items.stem: He did not so much refuse the assignment as shirk it, arriving late to every meeting at which it might have been discussed.

options.B: hand it on to a colleague

explanation.clue: 'Not so much refuse … as shirk' tells you the word is a milder, sneakier cousin of refusing; the lateness to meetings shows what that looks like.
explanation.correct_reasoning: To shirk is to evade a responsibility without confronting it. The sentence contrasts open refusal with the quiet avoidance the lateness demonstrates.

distractors.why_wrong: The sentence explicitly says he did not refuse; shirking is the quieter thing the contrast introduces.
Delegating would be an action; the sentence shows only absence and lateness, no handing on.
Arriving late to every relevant meeting is the opposite of completing the assignment early.

explanation.method: 'Not so much X as Y' places Y next to X on a scale. Decide which direction the scale runs — here, from open refusal toward quiet evasion — and pick the sense at Y's position.

items.stem: The proposal languished in a subcommittee for two years, neither rejected nor advanced.

explanation.clue: 'Neither rejected nor advanced' describes a proposal that nothing is happening to — a state of neglect, not of attack or decay.
explanation.correct_reasoning: To languish, of a document or plan, is to sit unattended without progress. The two-year stay and the double negative confirm stagnation rather than any active treatment.

distractors.why_wrong: Debate would be activity; the sentence describes the absence of any decision or movement.
Suppression implies someone acting against the proposal; languishing implies nobody acting at all, which is what 'neither rejected nor advanced' says.
Languish can mean to lose vigour, but the sentence reports the proposal's procedural status, not any change in its quality.

explanation.method: A word with several senses is fixed by its subject. Ask what kind of thing languishes here — a proposal in a committee — and choose the sense that applies to that kind of thing.

items.stem: The spokesman's answer was glib: fluent, reassuring, and wholly unresponsive to the question that had been asked.

options.A: smooth and fluent but shallow or insincere

explanation.clue: The colon introduces a three-part gloss: fluent, reassuring, unresponsive. Fluency plus emptiness is the definition.
explanation.correct_reasoning: Glib speech is easy and confident on the surface and hollow underneath. The sentence supplies both halves — the fluency and the failure to answer.

distractors.why_wrong: 'Wholly unresponsive to the question' rules out thoroughness; the answer sounded good and said nothing.
The answer was 'reassuring', which is the opposite of rude; glib fluency soothes rather than offends.
The sentence calls the answer fluent, which excludes hesitation.

explanation.method: When a colon is followed by a list of qualities, the word means the combination of them. Keep every item on the list; an option that fits only one of the three is a decoy.

items.stem: Her expression remained inscrutable throughout the verdict, so that even her counsel could not tell whether she had expected it.

explanation.clue: The result clause — 'so that even her counsel could not tell' — describes a face that gives nothing away. The prefix in- ('not') on a root meaning 'to examine closely' points the same way.
explanation.correct_reasoning: Inscrutable means not able to be understood or read. The sentence's consequence — nobody could tell what she felt — is the meaning restated.

distractors.why_wrong: A calm face might be readable as calm; the sentence's point is that her counsel could read nothing at all, not that she looked composed.
Open distress would be exactly what a counsel could tell; the sentence says the opposite.
This borrows 'scrutinise' from the same root and forgets the prefix: in-scrutable is what cannot be scrutinised, not what was.

explanation.method: A 'so that' clause states the effect of the word. Read the effect first; then, if the word has recognisable parts, check the prefix — 'in-' usually means 'not' — to confirm the direction.

items.stem: The treaty rested on reciprocity: each port would admit the other's ships on exactly the terms it asked for its own.

options.A: a mutual exchange of equivalent privileges
options.B: a generous concession by the stronger party
options.C: a favour granted without expecting any return
options.D: formal recognition of each other's sovereignty

explanation.clue: After the colon the sentence spells out the arrangement: each side gives what it asks — the same terms both ways.
explanation.correct_reasoning: Reciprocity is a relationship in which each party grants the other what it receives. 'Each port … on exactly the terms it asked for its own' is that symmetry described.

distractors.why_wrong: A concession is one-sided; the sentence describes both ports giving and getting the same terms.
The whole point of the arrangement is the expected return — each admits the other on matching terms.
The sentence concerns terms of admission for ships, not sovereignty.

explanation.method: Where a sentence says 'X: [an arrangement described in full]', the description after the colon is the definition of X. Test each option against that description, word by word.

items.stem: His congratulations were sardonic: he had, after all, predicted the failure of the scheme and now watched it succeed.

options.C: mocking in a dry, scornful way

explanation.clue: 'After all' explains the tone by the situation: a man who foretold failure and was proved wrong. Congratulations from him are unlikely to be simple; the sentence invites you to hear the edge in them.
explanation.correct_reasoning: Sardonic describes humour that is dry, mocking and a little bitter. The situation — congratulating a success he had predicted would fail — is exactly the kind that produces it.

distractors.why_wrong: The sentence's 'after all' sets up an explanation for something less than sincere; warmth would need no explaining.
Reluctance captures the discomfort but not the mockery; sardonic congratulations carry a barb, and the situation supplies one.
Nothing in the sentence concerns volume or exuberance; the tone is explained by wounded prediction, not by enthusiasm.

explanation.method: When a sentence explains a tone by a situation ('after all, he had…'), reconstruct the feeling the situation would produce and choose the word that names it, at the right strength.
